candidateRows: Ethical pronouncements express attitudes or commands rather than truth-apt propositions about objective moral facts.
This supplies the principal skeptical account of ethical language that the moral-landscape position must displace or accommodate.
O'Connor introduces his broad allegiance to emotivism and explains moral speech as expressive or directive rather than objectively true or false.
Emotivism treats a moral utterance as the expression of a feeling, not as a factual report that the speaker has that feeling.
The distinction prevents emotivism from being recast as an ordinary subjective proposition with an objective truth value.
Harris's attempted translation of emotivism into a factual statement about how a person feels.
O'Connor distinguishes expressing disapproval from reporting disapproval, preserving the non-truth-apt character of moral language under his view.
Possible conscious experiences form a landscape extending beyond current preferences, with factual routes between radically better and worse states.
This is the central positive case that facts about possible experience and causal navigation can ground substantive evaluative guidance.
O'Connor's claim that subjective preference plus instrumental choice exhausts the relevant story.
Harris expands from individual preference to unknown possible experiences, differences in experiential quality, and converging scientific knowledge about moving among them.
Science can identify how to reach a desired experiential peak while the desire to reach it remains a subjective preference.
It grants Harris's instrumental scientific claims while denying that those claims establish an objective normative destination.
Harris's argument that factual scientific inquiry can guide navigation across possible conscious experiences.
O'Connor separates empirical knowledge about effective means from the subjective preference that selects an experiential outcome as the destination.
Because inherited preference weights can themselves be scientifically altered, their contingent starting configuration cannot simply settle what experiences should be pursued.
The move challenges the skeptic's reliance on present preferences by making those preferences another variable requiring evaluation.
O'Connor's proposal that subjective preferences select ends while science supplies only the means to reach them.
Harris notes that preferences arise from unchosen causes and imagines a mature science capable of changing them, reopening the question of desirable change.
Even voluntary preference enhancement can be explained by higher-order preferences without introducing moral goodness, obligation, or prescription.
This directly answers the preference-malleability challenge by extending the subjective model to choices about which preferences to acquire.
Harris's suggestion that changing contingent preferences creates a further question about what one should become.
O'Connor uses an imagined enhancement of musical enjoyment to argue that second-order desire and scientific optimization still yield no moral judgment.
Failure to recognize unknown attainable goods may reflect empirical cognitive, emotional, or cultural closure rather than the absence of evaluative facts.
It shifts the dispute from preferred vocabulary to whether agents can be systematically closed off from substantially better available lives.
O'Connor's claim that preference modification and experiential improvement contain no moral judgment or prescription.
Harris argues that people can fail to know how good life could become and that their resistance to normative language may accompany remediable forms of closure.
Conscious systems have subjective values, while objective facts concern how best to achieve whatever those systems subjectively value.
This is the skeptic's core distinction between subjective ends and objective instrumental facts, directly opposing the proposed grounding of morality.
Harris's descriptive appeal to a value-laden landscape of better and worse conscious experiences.
O'Connor grants objective truths about conscious systems and effective action but locates value itself in each system's subjective commitments.
Calling value subjective does not deflate it, because some realities exist essentially as appearances in consciousness and resist reduction to external physical descriptions.
The move blocks the inference from phenomenal subjectivity to evaluative unreality, protecting conscious experience as a factual basis for the pro position.
O'Connor's distinction between subjective value and objective facts about the means of satisfying it.
Harris argues that the first-person mode of existence of conscious value does not make it less real or reducible away by physical description.
A complete account of preference, cooperation, discovery, and scientifically informed flourishing can still omit any objective moral truth.
This consolidates the con case by claiming explanatory completeness for subjective ends and instrumental science without objective morality.
Harris's claim that the reality and possible improvement of conscious experience supplies everything normatively important.
O'Connor constructs a social-development scenario driven by preferences, cooperation, openness, and increasing pleasure, then argues that objective moral truth remains absent.
Filling out the practical details of conscious life reveals objectively right and wrong ways to navigate possible experience toward greater well-being and away from misery.
The move directly argues that facts about possible conscious experience supply objective answers about well-being, addressing the central grounding dispute.
O'Connor's desert-island picture in which preferences and instrumental cooperation exhaust the explanation without objective moral truth.

After O'Connor asks what his preference-based picture omits, Harris argues that even one or two people face a navigation problem with demonstrably different experiential outcomes governed by discoverable natural facts.
